fetched_contents.text: A financial network perspective of financial institutions’ systemic risk contributions Highlights * • We measure systemic risk contribution by dynamic conditional correlation multivariate GARCH model. * • We construct minimum spanning trees (MSTs) from dynamic conditional correlations (DCC). * • We show the dynamic evolution of systemic risk contribution and financial network structure. * • We investigate quantitative relationships between systemic risk contribution and financial network structure. Abstract This study considers the effects of the financial institutions’ local topology structure in the financial network on their systemic risk contribution using data from the Chinese stock market. We first measure the systemic risk contribution with the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CoVaR) which is estimated by applying dynamic conditional correlation multivariate GARCH model (DCC-MVGARCH). Financial networks are constructed from dynamic conditional correlations (DCC) with graph filtering method of minimum spanning trees (MSTs). Then we investigate dynamics of systemic risk contributions of financial institution. Also we study dynamics of financial institution’s local topology structure in the financial network. Finally, we analyze the quantitative relationships between the local topology structure and systemic risk contribution with panel data regression analysis. We find that financial institutions with greater node strength, larger node betweenness centrality, larger node closeness centrality and larger node clustering coefficient tend to be associated with larger systemic risk contributions. Introduction The financial crisis has raised questions about the adequacy of financial regulation to ensure stability of the financial system. A particular feature was the threat of systemic risk [1]. According to the Bank for International Settlements, systemic risk in the financial system is the risk that a failure of a participant to meet its contractual obligations may in turn cause other participants to default, with the chain reaction leading to broader financial difficulties [2]. The related studies mainly focus on the measurement of financial institutions’ systemic risk contributions, influence factors of systemic risk contribution, and risk contagions among financial institutions [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [1]. Measuring the contribution of each financial institution to overall systemic risk can help identify the institution that contributes more to systemic risk. Stricter regulatory requirements for institutions with larger systemic risk contributions would break the tendency to generate systemic risk. Adrian and Brunnermeier [3] proposed CoVaR measure for systemic risk, namely the value at risk (VaR) of the financial system conditional on institutions being under distress. The authors defined an institution’s contribution to systemic risk as the difference between CoVaR conditional on the institution being under distress and the CoVaR in the median state of the institution. Other systemic risk contribution evaluations include Shapley value methodology and systemic expected shortfall (SES) [4], [5]. The influence factors of financial institutions’ systemic risk contribution mainly include institutional characteristics, such as size, leverage, maturity mismatch, etc. [3]. The failure of one institution spreading to other institutions results from financial links between them. These financial links include interbank loans, payment systems or OTC derivatives positions. Such an intricate structure of linkages can be captured by a network representation of the financial system. More recent studies explicitly model the financial links between institutions as networks and employ empirical or simulation techniques to assess the propagation of institution failures [1], [9], [10], [11]. These networks include interbank networks, payment networks, counter party exposures in credit default swaps, or trade credits between companies [12], [13], [14], [15]. However, the network analysis literature only concentrate on the effects of overall network structure on systemic risk. The relationships between institutions’ local network structure and systemic risk contributions are neglected. Furthermore, the stock price cross-correlations among financial institutions evaluate the systemic risk [16]. Such correlations are frequently used to construct financial networks. The research includes basic topology characteristics and intrinsic hierarchical structure of stock correlation network, etc. [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]. But the stock price cross-correlation network analyses rarely relate systemic risk contributions to financial institutions’ local structure. Our aim is to investigate the relationships between systemic risk contributions and institutions’ local topology structure in the financial networks. We first measure dynamic systemic risk contribution of financial institutions by estimating the change of CoVaR denoted by ΔCoVaR. Then dynamic minimum spanning trees (MST) of stock price cross-correlation are constructed from the dynamic conditional correlations (DCC). Finally, we use panel data regression, and relate these time-varying ΔCoVaRs to measures of each institution’s local network structures like node strength, node betweenness centrality, node closeness centrality, node occupation layer, and node clustering coefficient. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses relevant literature. Section 3 outlines the systemic risk contribution measures. Section 4 constructs financial networks and studies properties of the local network structure. Section 5 is the empirical study. The last section presents conclusion. Vouldis2 Abstract The analysis of contagion in financial networks has primarily focused on transmission channels operating through direct linkages. This paper develops a model of financial contagion in the interbank market featuring both direct and indirect transmission mechanisms. The model is used to analyse how shocks originating from outside sectors impact the functioning of the interbank market and investigates the emergence of instability in this setting. We conduct simulations on actual interbank bilateral exposures, constructed manually from a supervisory dataset reported by the largest euro area banks. We find that while the impact of direct contagion increases gradually with the shock intensity, the effect of indirect contagion is subject to threshold effects and can increase abruptly when the threshold is exceeded. In addition, the risk posed by indirect contagion has a higher upper bound compared to direct contagion. Finally, we find that in terms of overall impact, the shocks to the value of sovereign debt and non-bank financial institutions represent the most significant risk to the functioning of the interbank market. Risk can be transmitted within an interconnected financial system through both direct contagion channels, i.e., due to contractual obligations present between economic agents, and indirect mechanisms such as fire sales leading to depressed asset values and impacting banks' balance sheets, risk realisation in correlated portfolios, asymmetric information and the updating of imperfect information or beliefs. In addition, risk transmission depends significantly on the topology of the network formed by the contractual links between financial institutions. This paper builds a model of financial contagion that incorporates both direct and indirect contagion mechanisms and is calibrated on actual interbank data. Specifically, the model features sector-specific shocks both on the asset and the liability side, the hoarding of existing interbank funding as a response to liquidity strains while also featuring pro-cyclical haircuts and time-varying risk aversion that operate across the banking network. The analysis is grounded on an actual network of liquidity interconnections constructed based on supervisory data reported by all significant institutions (SIs) of the euro area countries as these institutions are designated by the European Central Bank (ECB), i.e., mainly large and interconnected credit institutions. Overall, we find that the impact of indirect contagion features a relatively large additional impact for a relatively small increase in the shock intensity, for example in the case of shocks to the government sector. Furthermore, the relative contributions of direct and indirect contagion are negatively correlated, with that of indirect contagion exceeding direct contagion for large values of the shock intensity. In addition, the upper bound of impact due to indirect contagion is significantly higher compared to that of direct contagion and can potentially affect the whole network. Overall, indirect contagion has the potential to substantially dominate the contagion phenomenon, especially during most severe shocks. This conclusion casts doubt in the focus on transmission channels propagating only through contractual connections that features in much of the existing literature. In addition, our results have important implications for the design of macro-prudential policy pointing to the need for focusing on indirect contagion channels. ECB Working Paper Series No 2883 2 1. fetched_contents.text: China’s shadow banking in 2020–2022: an empirical study Introduction Shadow banking has received continuous attention from both academia and the broad public. As the most apparent driving force behind the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), it came under elaborate scrutiny by global financial regulators. With the announcement of Basel III in 2010 to 2011, as well as other strict financial regulations (such as the Dodd-Frank Act in the U.S.), the development of shadow banking, which has been one very important supplicant to traditional commercial banks, seems to be slowing across the globe. Does shadow banking hide in the background because of the strengthened regulation? Two banking crises in 2023 remind us that this is not the case. One is Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) in the U.S., which mismatched the heavily weighted bond investment portfolio with unstable large amounts of corporate deposits. The other is Credit Suisse in Switzerland, which was involved in several high-profile risky transactions and investments and internal control loopholes. It maintained an investment-bank-style business portfolio and became inundated with scandals and litigationsFootnote 1. Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse operated similarly to the modus operandi of shadow banking. Asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control all contributed to imploding U.S. shadow banking in 2007–2008. They directly doomed the last remnants of investment banks, such as Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns. These elements again contributed to the demise of not-so-systematically-important SVB and G-SIFI Credit Suisse. The tricky part is that SVB and Credit Suisse both incorporated as banking institutions and followed strict banking regulations, including the complete evolving set of Basel III. In many ways, these banks exhibited characteristics of off-balance sheet shadow banking activities before 2008, which is both coincidence and irony. Research on systemic risk based on multi-layer financial networks is relatively scarce, and studies usually focus on only one type of risk. This paper develops a model of the multi-layer financial network system based on three types of links: firm-bank credit, asset-bank portfolio, and interbank lending, which simulates systemic risk under three risk sources: firm credit default, asset depreciation, and bank bankruptcy. The impact of the multi-layer financial network structure, default risk threshold, and bank asset allocation strategy is further explored. It has been shown that the larger the risk shock, the greater the systemic risk under different risk sources, and the risk propagation cycle tends to rise and then decline. As centralized nodes in the multi-layer financial network system, bank nodes may play both blocking and propagation roles under different risk sources. Furthermore, the multi-layer financial network system is most susceptible to bank bankruptcy risk, followed by firm credit default risk. Further research indicates that increasing the average degree of firms in the bank–firm credit network, the density of the bank-asset portfolio network, and the bank capital adequacy ratio all contribute to reducing systemic risk under the three risk sources. Due to the complexity of the financial system, complex network theory has been utilized to study financial risk to fully understand the complex connections among the components of the financial system, as well as to investigate the mechanisms involved in the generation and propagation of financial risk within the whole complex system. Under the impact of COVID-19, and in the context of current deeper economic globalization, the links among agents in the financial system have become more closely linked, and the types of links have also become more diverse, providing more channels for the spread of financial risks. In this paper, three agents in the financial system are fully considered: banks, assets, and firms. It constructs a multi-layer financial network system model based on bank–firm credit linkages, bank-asset portfolio linkages, and interbank lending linkages, and investigates the systemic risk of the multi-layer financial network system through numerical simulation. Since different financial network systems typically have distinct structural characteristics, some studies have empirically analyzed the structural characteristics of interbank networks by utilizing actual interbank data. Several empirical studies have demonstrated that interbank networks exhibit characteristics of small-world networks or scale-free networks [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19]. Branch report on the empirical and institutional context of financial relationships

The evidence points to a financial system in China where shadow banking and interbank markets are central, but regulated in ways that shape the types of relationships and exposures. The most commonly linked institutions and instruments are shadow banking entities and traditional financial institutions, especially commercial banks, with strong ties to interbank lending, bond holdings, and off-balance-sheet financing. The shadow banking study notes that China’s shadow banking reached RMB 47.6 trillion by the end of 2022, with a large share of assets held in bonds and a clientele profile focused on underserved sectors such as infrastructure investment and real estate enterprises [N4-F3]. It also emphasizes that shadow banking often bypasses traditional banking regulations and operates outside of them, which suggests a system where regulated and non-regulated financial linkages coexist [N4-R2]. The same study compares China’s shadow banking to U.S. shadow banking-like institutions such as SVB and Credit Suisse, noting similar exposure to bond investment and balance-sheet mismatch [N4-F3]. This implies that in China the most common financial relationships are not just between commercial banks but also between shadow banking vehicles and credit recipients, with bonds, WMPs, and trust financing as important instruments [N4-F3].

The regulatory context is shaped by both shadow banking controls and broader financial regulation. The evidence shows that institutions were explicitly prohibited from using cash management WMPs to finance credit or lending activities that would bypass regulatory restrictions [N4-R3]. It also notes that shadow banking has been a major object of global regulatory attention since the 2008 crisis, with Basel III and other regulations slowing its global growth, yet the 2023 banking crises suggest that regulatory barriers do not fully eliminate systemic vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. The shadow banking paper further highlights that regulatory scrutiny and tightening can reduce apparent growth, but shadow banking may still remain a significant source of financial stability concerns because it often lacks deposit guarantees and central bank liquidity backstop [N4-F3]. In the institutional setting, shadow banking appears to be a shadow finance layer that interacts with traditional banking through interbank and repo-like mechanisms, while regulators attempt to constrain it through WMP restrictions and monitoring frameworks [N4-R4].

Empirically, the evidence supports a pattern in which stronger relationships are associated with greater risk spillovers. The study on interbank lending and systemic risk in China uses the HITS algorithm to analyze network structure and explores the influence of nonbanking institutions [N1-R1]. Another study proposes a DAG-based framework for generalized variance decomposition to investigate heterogeneous return spillovers, showing that network structure and interconnectedness matter for risk transmission [N1-R2]. A third study finds that indirect linkages contribute more to systemic risk than direct linkages, and that different shocks can produce different systemic risk outcomes [N1-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that financial relationships that are more concentrated, more interconnected, or more indirect are more likely to transmit risk. The shadow banking evidence also supports this: shadow banking’s large bond holdings and balance-sheet mismatch make it vulnerable in distress, and its exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing means it can spill over to non-banks and small regional banks [N4-F3]. So the empirical pattern is that stronger, more indirect, and more concentrated relationships—whether in interbank lending, repo, or shadow banking—are associated with larger risk spillovers.

Overall, the institutional context is one of regulated banking coexisting with shadow banking, with interbank and bond-based linkages as the main channels. The regulatory framework tries to limit risky financing and WMP use, but the evidence suggests that even regulated institutions can resemble shadow banking in their business model and vulnerability structure [N4-F3]. The empirical literature indicates that networked relationships—especially those involving indirect exposures, high centrality, and concentration—tend to amplify systemic risk [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

Branch report on risk transmission channels and relationship types

The evidence identifies three main transmission channels: interbank lending, repo, and securitization, each with distinct risk mechanisms. For interbank lending, the ECB paper notes that risk can be transmitted through direct contagion channels due to contractual obligations, but also through indirect mechanisms such as fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes that interbank lending helps banks manage liquidity risk, but also creates vulnerabilities because of the contractual links and the network topology [N3-R3]. The evidence therefore suggests that interbank lending transmits risk by both direct contractual obligations and indirect network effects, with contagion intensity depending on the strength of the shock and the network structure [N3-F2][N3-R3].

For repo, the evidence is indirect but still informative. The ECB paper itself does not directly discuss repo, but it does describe the broader mechanism of collateralized and unsecured interbank markets, where secured and unsecured markets function differently in the presence of credit risk [N3-R4]. The paper also notes that risk transmission can involve liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts, which are especially relevant when institutions face liquidity strains [N3-F2]. While repo is not explicitly modeled here, the collateral and liquidity structure implied by the evidence supports the idea that repo-like transactions can transmit risk through collateral depreciation and liquidity reallocation, especially when institutions have high exposures and face funding stress [N3-R4][N3-F2].

For securitization, the evidence is again indirect but very relevant. The “Securitized Banking and the Run on Repo” paper uses a novel dataset on securitized bonds to trace the path of crisis from subprime-housing related assets into broader markets [N3-R2]. This implies that securitization can transmit risk through asset-backed claims and structured products, with contagion occurring as asset values fall and investors or counterparties become exposed to defaults or liquidity runs [N3-R2]. The broader ECB paper similarly notes that fire sales and depressed asset values can feed into bank balance sheets and risk realization in correlated portfolios, reinforcing the idea that securitized assets can serve as a conduit for risk propagation [N3-F2]. So the evidence supports a view of securitization as a channel where risk moves from underlying collateralized assets into the repo or trading markets, then spreads through interconnected institutions.

The evidence also shows how different loan types and collateral structures change contagion patterns. The ECB paper stresses that secured and unsecured markets function differently under credit risk, with safe collateral, for example, affecting the risk profile of interbank exposures [N3-R4]. The shadow banking study adds that shadow banking often relies on bond holdings and trust financing, and that its balance-sheet mismatch and exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing make it vulnerable in distress [N4-F3]. This means that collateralized lending tends to reduce direct contagion, while unsecured or highly leveraged lending increases vulnerability. The multi-layer financial network study further shows that when banks hold more assets in a single market, they become more vulnerable to that market’s risks [N5-F4]. So the contagion pattern is not uniform: secured or diversified collateral structures can dampen propagation, while concentrated or unsecured exposures can amplify it.

Liquidity and information asymmetry are repeatedly identified as amplifiers of systemic effects. The ECB paper explicitly states that liquidity hoarding, pro-cyclical haircuts, and time-varying risk aversion operate across the banking network [N3-F2]. It also notes that asymmetric information and updating imperfect information or beliefs are key indirect contagion mechanisms [N3-F2]. The shadow banking study similarly points to asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control as vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. These factors combine to make liquidity shocks and information gaps especially dangerous. When institutions face liquidity strains, they may hoard funding, raise haircuts, and propagate risk more rapidly [N3-F2]. When information is incomplete or asymmetric, institutions may misprice risks or fail to update beliefs correctly, which can trigger cascading failures [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a view in which liquidity stress and information asymmetry do not just add noise; they can significantly magnify systemic effects by making contagion more abrupt and harder to contain.

In summary, the risk transmission channels in the evidence are interbank lending (direct and indirect), repo-like collateral and liquidity mechanisms, and securitization-based asset-backed contagion. Different loan types and collateral structures alter contagion patterns: secured and diversified exposures tend to reduce propagation, while unsecured or concentrated exposures amplify it. Liquidity stress and information asymmetry are especially important because they can turn modest shocks into systemic amplification through hoarding, haircuts, and belief updating [N3-F2][N3-R4][N4-F3].

Branch report on systemic risk measurement and modeling frameworks

The evidence identifies several risk measures that are best suited to capturing interconnectedness and failure propagation. CoVaR is a prominent one: the financial network paper states that systemic risk contribution is measured with CoVaR, estimated by applying dynamic conditional correlation multivariate GARCH (DCC-MVGARCH) [N2-R1][N2-F1]. It also notes that CoVaR is defined as the value at risk of the financial system conditional on institutions being under distress [N2-F1]. Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and delta CoVaR are also mentioned in the systematic risk review literature [N2-R2]. In addition, the network paper highlights that financial institutions’ local topology structure affects their systemic risk contribution, and that node strength, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and clustering coefficient are all associated with larger systemic risk contributions [N2-R3][N2-F1]. This suggests that network-based measures such as centrality metrics are useful for capturing interconnectedness, while CoVaR-like measures capture the conditional tail risk of the entire system.

Network-based models differ from traditional VaR/CVaR approaches in two main ways. First, they explicitly model the structure of financial linkages and how those linkages propagate risk across the system. The financial network paper says that financial links are represented as a network, and that empirical or simulation techniques are used to assess failure propagation [N2-F1]. It also notes that the network literature has concentrated on the effects of overall network structure, but that local topology structure and systemic risk contributions have been underexplored [N2-F1]. Second, network models can capture indirect contagion and the role of network topology, whereas traditional VaR and CVaR approaches typically focus on the distributional properties of individual institutions or portfolios [N2-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that indirect contagion can have a much larger upper bound and can dominate contagion effects during severe shocks, which traditional VaR/CVaR approaches may not fully reflect [N3-F2]. Thus, network models are better suited to understanding how interconnectedness and network structure shape systemic risk, while traditional measures are more limited to aggregate risk quantification.

Distinguishing direct contagion from indirect macroeconomic effects is important because the evidence shows that contagion is not always purely internal. The ECB paper explicitly distinguishes direct contagion channels due to contractual obligations from indirect mechanisms such as fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs [N3-F2]. It also notes that the impact of indirect contagion can be subject to threshold effects and can increase abruptly when thresholds are exceeded, while direct contagion increases gradually with shock intensity [N3-F2]. The same paper states that shocks to sovereign debt and non-bank financial institutions are among the most significant risks to the functioning of the interbank market [N3-F2]. This implies that direct contagion is driven by the network of contractual exposures and funding dependencies, while indirect effects can emerge from broader macroeconomic shocks, asset price declines, and information frictions. The network paper further distinguishes systemic risk contribution from the network structure, showing that local topology matters in addition to macroeconomic conditions [N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered approach: CoVaR and delta CoVaR are useful for tail risk and conditional systemic risk, while network-based measures such as minimum spanning trees and local topology metrics help capture interconnectedness and failure propagation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1]. Traditional VaR/CVaR approaches are less effective at capturing indirect contagion and the role of network structure, which is why network models are better suited to systemic risk assessment in highly interconnected systems [N2-F1][N3-F2]. Direct contagion is tied to contractual obligations and funding links, while indirect contagion and macroeconomic effects arise from asset values, information asymmetry, and broader systemic shocks [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore provides a clear framework for choosing risk measures and distinguishing between direct and indirect sources of systemic risk.

Branch report on multilayer and dynamic contagion mechanisms

The evidence shows that multilayer models represent different financial linkages and exposures by explicitly separating multiple types of connections within the same system. The multi-layer financial network study constructs a model based on three types of links: firm-bank credit, asset-bank portfolio, and interbank lending [N5-R2][N5-F4]. It then simulates systemic risk under three risk sources: firm credit default, asset depreciation, and bank bankruptcy [N5-F4]. This is a clear example of a multilayer representation: each layer captures a distinct financial relationship, so the model can assess how risk spreads through credit, portfolio, and interbank channels simultaneously [N5-F4]. The same paper also notes that financial risk can be spread directly between banks through interbank lending, but that different financial network systems typically have distinct structural characteristics [N5-F4]. This suggests that multilayer models are useful because they avoid the limitations of single-layer analyses and instead capture the full diversity of exposures in a financial system [N5-F4].

Dynamic contagion evolves over time and depends heavily on network structure. The ECB paper emphasizes that its model aims to capture dynamics evolving during crisis rather than tranquil times, and highlights mechanisms such as liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts [N6-R5]. It also states that the impact of indirect contagion can feature threshold effects and can increase abruptly when the threshold is exceeded, while direct contagion increases gradually with shock intensity [N3-F2]. The dynamic multi-layer financial network paper similarly finds that the larger the risk shock, the greater the systemic risk under different risk sources, and that the risk propagation cycle tends to rise and then decline [N5-F4]. This indicates that contagion is not static: it can intensify, then stabilize, and then potentially fade, depending on the shock magnitude and the network structure. The evidence further shows that bank nodes can play both blocking and propagation roles under different risk sources, and that the density of the bank-asset portfolio network, the average degree of firms, and the bank capital adequacy ratio all affect systemic risk [N5-F4]. These findings suggest that dynamic contagion depends not only on the initial shock but also on the evolving network topology and the institutions’ internal characteristics.

Agent-based and BiMM approaches simulate systemic failure propagation by modeling the behavior and interactions of individual agents in a dynamic network. The agent-based multi-layer network simulation paper addresses measuring systemic risk and identifying SIFIs using agent-based methods [N5-R1]. The agent-based model for financial vulnerability paper develops a structure for an agent-based model to provide a system-wide view of agents’ transformations and dynamic interactions [N5-R4]. The multi-layered interbank model paper develops an agent-based multi-layered interbank network model based on a sample of large EU banks [N5-R3]. The multi-agent-based interbank lending network paper generates a dynamic network through a bidirectional matching mechanism (BiMM) [N5-R5]. Together, these sources show that agent-based models simulate systemic failure by representing institutions as agents with rules for behavior, funding, defaulting, and recovery, and by allowing the network to evolve over time [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. BiMM adds a dynamic network generation mechanism, so it can represent both the structure and the time-varying nature of interbank relationships [N5-R5].

The evidence also suggests that multilayer and dynamic models are especially suited to capturing complex contagion patterns. The multi-layer financial network study shows that the system is most susceptible to bank bankruptcy risk, followed by firm credit default risk, and that increasing the density of the bank-asset portfolio network and the capital adequacy ratio can reduce systemic risk [N5-F4]. The dynamic multi-layer financial network paper also finds that the more assets a bank holds in a single market, the more vulnerable it is to the risks associated with that market [N5-F4]. This implies that contagion is not only a matter of network topology but also of asset concentration and exposure diversification. The ECB paper further shows that indirect contagion can dominate during severe shocks, and that liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts amplify propagation [N3-F2]. These findings support the use of multilayer and dynamic models to study how contagion evolves across layers and over time, rather than relying on static snapshots or single-layer assumptions [N5-F4][N5-R5][N3-F2].

In conclusion, multilayer models represent different financial linkages and exposures by separating firm-bank, asset-bank, and interbank layers [N5-R2][N5-F4]. Dynamic contagion evolves over time and depends on network structure, shock magnitude, liquidity conditions, and institutional characteristics [N3-F2][N5-F4]. Agent-based and BiMM approaches simulate systemic failure propagation by representing agents, dynamic interactions, and evolving network structures [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a modeling strategy in which multilayer and dynamic approaches are the most appropriate tools for understanding how risk propagates through interconnected financial systems.

## Integrated final answer on the link between financial institution relationships and systemic risk

The evidence from the four branch reports supports a clear conclusion: **the relationships among Chinese financial institutions are central to systemic risk, and the structure of those relationships determines how risk spreads, amplifies, and can become catastrophic**. The system is not just a collection of banks; it includes shadow banking, interbank lending, repo-like mechanisms, securitization, and broader multilayer exposures. The key is that **stronger, more interconnected, and more indirect relationships are more likely to generate systemic spillovers**, while the regulatory and institutional context shapes both the nature of those relationships and the risk mitigation tools available [N4-F3][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 1. Which financial institutions and instruments are most commonly linked in the Chinese system?

The evidence points to a system dominated by **shadow banking and interbank markets**, with **commercial banks, trust financing, bond holdings, WMPs, and interbank lending** as the most common linkages [N4-F3][N1-R1]. Shadow banking, in particular, is described as a major channel for financing underserved sectors such as **infrastructure investment and real estate enterprises**, and it often bypasses traditional banking regulations [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The same study notes that **bond investment accounts for a large share of shadow banking assets** and that **SVB-style institutions** have a similar business model, with heavy bond exposure and balance-sheet mismatch [N4-F3]. This suggests that the most common financial relationships in China are not only between commercial banks but also between shadow banking entities and credit recipients, with bonds, trust financing, and repo-like funding as the main instruments [N4-F3].

The interbank lending literature further shows that **interbank networks are the primary empirical focus**, and that the structure of these networks is often analyzed using **direct and indirect contagion mechanisms** [N1-R1][N3-F2]. The evidence also implies that **securitization and asset-backed lending** are important transmission channels, because they can bundle risks into structured products and then spread them through interconnected institutions [N3-R2][N3-R4]. In short, the Chinese financial system is best understood as a **hybrid of regulated and shadow finance**, with **interbank lending, bond holdings, trust financing, WMPs, and securitized assets** as the dominant linkages [N4-F3][N1-R1][N3-R2].

### 2. How regulatory structures shape investment and lending behavior

Regulation plays a central role in shaping both the types of relationships and the risk profile of the system. The shadow banking evidence shows that institutions were explicitly prohibited from using **cash management WMPs to finance credit or lending activities that would bypass regulatory restrictions**, which indicates that regulators are trying to limit shadow finance while still allowing some non-bank financial activity [N4-R3]. It also notes that shadow banking has been a major object of global regulatory attention since the 2008 crisis, with **Basel III and other regulations slowing its global growth**, yet the 2023 banking crises suggest that regulatory barriers do not fully eliminate systemic vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. This means that the regulatory context is not simply one of suppression; it is one of **constraint and monitoring**, with shadow banking often operating at the edge of regulation [N4-R4].

The evidence further suggests that regulation influences investment and lending behavior through **asset-liability structure, collateral use, and liquidity management**. The shadow banking study highlights that **asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control** are vulnerabilities, implying that institutions can become risky if they are not properly regulated or if they rely on complex financing structures [N4-F3]. The ECB paper also shows that **secured and unsecured markets function differently under credit risk**, and that **collateral structure affects risk transmission** [N3-R4]. This means that regulatory choices around collateral, leverage, and liquidity management directly shape the stability of the system [N3-R4][N4-F3].

### 3. What empirical patterns link stronger relationships to risk spillovers?

The empirical evidence strongly supports the view that **stronger relationships are associated with greater risk spillovers**. The interbank lending study uses **network analysis and the HITS algorithm** to examine systemic risk, and the DAG-based framework study investigates **heterogeneous return spillovers** [N1-R1][N1-R2]. Another study finds that **indirect linkages contribute more to systemic risk than direct linkages**, and that different shocks produce different systemic risk outcomes [N1-R3]. These results suggest a clear empirical pattern: **the more interconnected a relationship network is, the more likely it is to generate systemic effects**.

The shadow banking evidence also supports this pattern. Because shadow banking often has **large bond holdings, balance-sheet mismatch, and exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing**, it is particularly vulnerable in distress and can spill over to non-banks and small regional banks [N4-F3]. The network literature further shows that **node strength, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and clustering coefficient** are all associated with larger systemic risk contributions [N2-R3][N2-F1]. In other words, institutions that are central, highly connected, or concentrated in the network are more likely to amplify risk. The evidence therefore supports a **network-based explanation of systemic risk**: stronger relationships, higher centrality, and more concentrated exposures are empirically linked to greater spillovers [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F1].

### 4. How systemic risk is measured and modeled

The evidence identifies several risk measures that are best suited to capturing interconnectedness and failure propagation. **CoVaR** is a central measure, as it estimates the **value at risk of the financial system conditional on institutions being under distress**, and the financial network paper uses **dynamic conditional correlation multivariate GARCH (DCC-MVGARCH)** to estimate it [N2-R1][N2-F1]. **Delta CoVaR** and **CVaR** are also mentioned in the systematic risk review literature [N2-R2]. These measures are useful because they capture **tail risk and conditional systemic risk**, which is important in a networked system [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Network-based models differ from traditional **VaR/CVaR approaches** in two important ways. First, they explicitly model the structure of financial linkages and how those linkages propagate risk across the system [N2-F1]. Second, they capture **indirect contagion and the role of network topology**, whereas traditional measures typically focus on the distributional properties of individual institutions or portfolios [N2-F1]. The ECB paper also notes that **indirect contagion can have a much larger upper bound** and can dominate contagion effects during severe shocks, which traditional VaR/CVaR approaches may not fully reflect [N3-F2]. Thus, network models are better suited to understanding how interconnectedness and network structure shape systemic risk [N2-F1][N3-F2].

The evidence also provides a clear way to distinguish **direct contagion from indirect macroeconomic effects**. Direct contagion occurs through **contractual obligations and funding dependencies**, while indirect contagion arises through **fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs** [N3-F2]. The ECB paper further states that shocks to **sovereign debt and non-bank financial institutions** are among the most significant risks to the functioning of the interbank market, showing that macroeconomic shocks can feed into systemic risk even when the initial trigger is not purely internal [N3-F2]. The network paper adds that local topology matters in addition to macroeconomic conditions, so the distinction is not only about whether the shock comes from inside or outside the system but also about how the network structure amplifies or dampens it [N2-F1].

### 5. Multilayer models: how they represent different financial linkages and exposures

Multilayer models are especially useful because they represent **different financial linkages and exposures separately**. The multi-layer financial network study constructs a model based on **three types of links**: **firm-bank credit, asset-bank portfolio, and interbank lending** [N5-R2][N5-F4]. It then simulates systemic risk under three risk sources: **firm credit default, asset depreciation, and bank bankruptcy** [N5-F4]. This is a clear example of a **multilayer representation**: each layer captures a distinct financial relationship, so the model can assess how risk spreads through credit, portfolio, and interbank channels simultaneously [N5-F4]. The same paper notes that financial risk can be spread directly between banks through interbank lending, but that different financial network systems typically have distinct structural characteristics [N5-F4]. This suggests that multilayer models are useful because they avoid the limitations of single-layer analyses and instead capture the full diversity of exposures in a financial system [N5-F4].

### 6. Dynamic contagion: how it evolves over time and depends on network structure

Dynamic contagion is not static; it evolves over time and depends heavily on **network structure, shock magnitude, liquidity conditions, and institutional characteristics**. The ECB paper emphasizes that its model aims to capture **dynamics evolving during crisis rather than tranquil times**, and highlights mechanisms such as **liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts** [N6-R5]. It also states that the impact of **indirect contagion can feature threshold effects and can increase abruptly when the threshold is exceeded**, while **direct contagion increases gradually with shock intensity** [N3-F2]. The dynamic multi-layer financial network paper similarly finds that the **larger the risk shock, the greater the systemic risk under different risk sources**, and that the **risk propagation cycle tends to rise and then decline** [N5-F4]. These findings indicate that contagion can intensify, stabilize, and then fade depending on the shock and the network structure.

The evidence also shows that **bank nodes can play both blocking and propagation roles under different risk sources**, and that **the density of the bank-asset portfolio network, the average degree of firms, and the bank capital adequacy ratio** all affect systemic risk [N5-F4]. This means that dynamic contagion depends not only on the initial shock but also on the evolving network topology and the institutions’ internal characteristics. The ECB paper further shows that **indirect contagion can dominate during severe shocks**, reinforcing the idea that contagion is a dynamic, threshold-sensitive process [N3-F2].

### 7. Agent-based and BiMM approaches: how they simulate systemic failure propagation

Agent-based and **BiMM (bidirectional matching mechanism)** approaches are particularly well suited to simulating systemic failure propagation because they model **behavior, interactions, and evolving network structures**. The agent-based multi-layer network simulation paper addresses **measuring systemic risk and identifying SIFIs using agent-based methods** [N5-R1]. The agent-based model for financial vulnerability paper develops a structure for an agent-based model to provide a **system-wide view of agents’ transformations and dynamic interactions** [N5-R4]. The multi-layered interbank model paper develops an **agent-based multi-layered interbank network model based on a sample of large EU banks** [N5-R3]. The multi-agent-based interbank lending network paper generates a **dynamic network through a bidirectional matching mechanism (BiMM)** [N5-R5]. Together, these sources show that agent-based models simulate systemic failure by representing institutions as agents with rules for behavior, funding, defaulting, and recovery, and by allowing the network to evolve over time [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

BiMM adds a **dynamic network generation mechanism**, so it can represent both the **structure and the time-varying nature** of interbank relationships [N5-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the use of agent-based and BiMM approaches to study how systemic failure propagates through interconnected financial systems, especially when the network is evolving and the failure process is nonlinear [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

### 8. Risk transmission channels and relationship types

The evidence identifies three main transmission channels: **interbank lending, repo, and securitization**, each with distinct risk mechanisms. For **interbank lending**, the ECB paper notes that risk can be transmitted through **direct contagion channels due to contractual obligations**, but also through **indirect mechanisms such as fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs** [N3-F2]. It also emphasizes that interbank lending helps banks manage liquidity risk, but also creates vulnerabilities because of the contractual links and the network topology [N3-R3]. This means that interbank lending transmits risk by both direct obligations and indirect network effects [N3-F2][N3-R3].

For **repo-like mechanisms**, the evidence is indirect but still informative. The ECB paper discusses **secured and unsecured interbank markets** and notes that they function differently under credit risk, with safe collateral affecting the risk profile of interbank exposures [N3-R4]. The paper also notes that liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts operate across the banking network [N3-F2]. While repo is not explicitly modeled here, the collateral and liquidity structure implied by the evidence supports the idea that repo-like transactions can transmit risk through collateral depreciation and liquidity reallocation, especially when institutions face liquidity strains [N3-R4][N3-F2].

For **securitization**, the evidence is again indirect but very relevant. The “Securitized Banking and the Run on Repo” paper uses a novel dataset on securitized bonds to trace the path of crisis from **subprime-housing related assets into broader markets** [N3-R2]. This implies that securitization can transmit risk through asset-backed claims and structured products, with contagion occurring as asset values fall and investors or counterparties become exposed to defaults or liquidity runs [N3-R2]. The broader ECB paper similarly notes that fire sales and depressed asset values can feed into bank balance sheets and risk realization in correlated portfolios, reinforcing the idea that securitized assets can serve as a conduit for risk propagation [N3-F2].

The evidence also shows how **different loan types and collateral structures change contagion patterns**. The ECB paper stresses that secured and unsecured markets function differently under credit risk, with safe collateral affecting interbank exposures [N3-R4]. The shadow banking study adds that shadow banking often relies on bond holdings and trust financing, and that its balance-sheet mismatch and exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing make it vulnerable in distress [N4-F3]. This means that **collateralized lending tends to reduce direct contagion**, while **unsecured or highly leveraged lending increases vulnerability**. The multi-layer financial network study further shows that when banks hold more assets in a single market, they become more vulnerable to that market’s risks [N5-F4]. So the contagion pattern is not uniform: **secured or diversified exposures tend to reduce propagation, while concentrated or unsecured exposures amplify it**.

Liquidity and information asymmetry are repeatedly identified as **amplifiers of systemic effects**. The ECB paper explicitly states that **liquidity hoarding, pro-cyclical haircuts, and time-varying risk aversion operate across the banking network** [N3-F2]. It also notes that **asymmetric information and updating imperfect information or beliefs** are key indirect contagion mechanisms [N3-F2]. The shadow banking study similarly points to **asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control** as vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. These factors combine to make liquidity shocks and information gaps especially dangerous. When institutions face liquidity strains, they may hoard funding, raise haircuts, and propagate risk more rapidly [N3-F2]. When information is incomplete or asymmetric, institutions may misprice risks or fail to update beliefs correctly, which can trigger cascading failures [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a view in which **liquidity stress and information asymmetry do not just add noise; they can significantly magnify systemic effects**.

### 9. Integrated synthesis: what this means for understanding systemic risk in China

Putting the evidence together, the strongest conclusion is that **systemic risk in China is fundamentally shaped by the structure of financial institution relationships**. The system is **interconnected, heterogeneous, and multilayered**, with shadow banking, interbank lending, repo-like mechanisms, and securitization as the main channels. The regulatory context shapes those relationships by constraining shadow finance, collateral use, and liquidity management [N4-F3][N4-R3][N3-R4]. The empirical evidence shows that **stronger, more indirect, and more concentrated relationships are more likely to generate systemic spillovers** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Network-based and multilayer models are therefore especially useful because they can capture both the **interconnectedness of the system** and the **different types of exposures** [N2-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence also suggests that **risk measurement should move beyond traditional VaR/CVaR approaches** and incorporate **CoVaR, network topology, and dynamic contagion mechanisms** [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Agent-based and BiMM approaches are especially powerful for simulating how systemic failure propagates through a network, because they can represent behavior, liquidity dynamics, and evolving network structures [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Finally, the evidence supports a **distinction between direct contagion and indirect macroeconomic effects**. Direct contagion is driven by **contractual obligations and funding links**, while indirect effects arise from **asset price declines, fire sales, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and broader macroeconomic shocks** [N3-F2]. This distinction is important because it means that systemic risk is not only a matter of financial network structure, but also of **how the network interacts with macroeconomic and informational conditions** [N3-F2][N2-F1].

### Conclusion

In sum, the evidence in the branch reports supports a **network-centric view of systemic risk in China**: stronger relationships, more indirect exposures, higher centrality, and more concentrated or unsecured linkages amplify risk spillovers, while regulatory constraints, collateral structure, liquidity management, and information quality shape the system’s stability [N4-F3][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F1][N3-F2]. The best modeling approaches are **network-based, multilayer, and dynamic**, because they can capture interconnectedness, failure propagation, and the evolving nature of contagion [N2-F1][N5-F4][N5-R5]. The evidence therefore provides a strong foundation for understanding **how investment and lending relationships among Chinese financial institutions generate systemic risk**, and for choosing the most appropriate risk measures and models in that context [N4-F3][N2-R1][N3-F2].

The ECB paper stresses that secured and unsecured markets function differently under credit risk, with safe collateral affecting interbank exposures [N3-R4]. The shadow banking study adds that shadow banking often relies on bond holdings and trust financing, and that its balance-sheet mismatch and exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing make it vulnerable in distress [N4-F3]. This means that **collateralized lending tends to reduce direct contagion**, while **unsecured or highly leveraged lending increases vulnerability**. The multi-layer financial network study further shows that when banks hold more assets in a single market, they become more vulnerable to that market’s risks [N5-F4]. So the contagion pattern is not uniform: **secured or diversified exposures tend to reduce propagation, while concentrated or unsecured exposures amplify it**.

Liquidity and information asymmetry are repeatedly identified as **amplifiers of systemic effects**. The ECB paper explicitly states that **liquidity hoarding, pro-cyclical haircuts, and time-varying risk aversion operate across the banking network** [N3-F2]. It also notes that **asymmetric information and updating imperfect information or beliefs** are key indirect contagion mechanisms [N3-F2]. The shadow banking study similarly points to **asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control** as vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. These factors combine to make liquidity shocks and information gaps especially dangerous. When institutions face liquidity strains, they may hoard funding, raise haircuts, and propagate risk more rapidly [N3-F2]. When information is incomplete or asymmetric, institutions may misprice risks or fail to update beliefs correctly, which can trigger cascading failures [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a view in which **liquidity stress and information asymmetry do not just add noise; they can significantly magnify systemic effects**.

### 9. Integrated synthesis: what this means for understanding systemic risk in China

Putting the evidence together, the strongest conclusion is that **systemic risk in China is fundamentally shaped by the structure of financial institution relationships**. The system is **interconnected, heterogeneous, and multilayered**, with shadow banking, interbank lending, repo-like mechanisms, and securitization as the main channels. The regulatory context shapes those relationships by constraining shadow finance, collateral use, and liquidity management [N4-F3][N4-R3][N3-R4]. The empirical evidence shows that **stronger, more indirect, and more concentrated relationships are more likely to generate systemic spillovers** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. Network-based and multilayer models are therefore especially useful because they can capture both the **interconnectedness of the system** and the **different types of exposures** [N2-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence also suggests that **risk measurement should move beyond traditional VaR/CVaR approaches** and incorporate **CoVaR, network topology, and dynamic contagion mechanisms** [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2]. Agent-based and BiMM approaches are especially powerful for simulating how systemic failure propagates through a network, because they can represent behavior, liquidity dynamics, and evolving network structures [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Finally, the evidence supports a **distinction between direct contagion and indirect macroeconomic effects**. Direct contagion is driven by **contractual obligations and funding links**, while indirect effects arise from **asset price declines, fire sales, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and broader macroeconomic shocks** [N3-F2]. This distinction is important because it means that systemic risk is not only a matter of financial network structure, but also of **how the network interacts with macroeconomic and informational conditions** [N3-F2][N2-F1].

### Conclusion

In sum, the evidence in the branch reports supports a **network-centric view of systemic risk in China**: stronger relationships, more indirect exposures, higher centrality, and more concentrated or unsecured linkages amplify risk spillovers, while regulatory constraints, collateral structure, liquidity management, and information quality shape the system’s stability [N4-F3][N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N2-F1][N3-F2]. The best modeling approaches are **network-based, multilayer, and dynamic**, because they can capture interconnectedness, failure propagation, and the evolving nature of contagion [N2-F1][N5-F4][N5-R5]. The evidence therefore provides a strong foundation for understanding **how investment and lending relationships among Chinese financial institutions generate systemic risk**, and for choosing the most appropriate risk measures and models in that context [N4-F3][N2-R1][N3-F2].

Branch report on the empirical and institutional context of financial relationships

The evidence points to a financial system in China where shadow banking and interbank markets are central, but regulated in ways that shape the types of relationships and exposures. The most commonly linked institutions and instruments are shadow banking entities and traditional financial institutions, especially commercial banks, with strong ties to interbank lending, bond holdings, and off-balance-sheet financing. The shadow banking study notes that China’s shadow banking reached RMB 47.6 trillion by the end of 2022, with a large share of assets held in bonds and a clientele profile focused on underserved sectors such as infrastructure investment and real estate enterprises [N4-F3]. It also emphasizes that shadow banking often bypasses traditional banking regulations and operates outside of them, which suggests a system where regulated and non-regulated financial linkages coexist [N4-R2]. The same study compares China’s shadow banking to U.S. shadow banking-like institutions such as SVB and Credit Suisse, noting similar exposure to bond investment and balance-sheet mismatch [N4-F3]. This implies that in China the most common financial relationships are not just between commercial banks but also between shadow banking vehicles and credit recipients, with bonds, WMPs, and trust financing as important instruments [N4-F3].

The regulatory context is shaped by both shadow banking controls and broader financial regulation. The evidence shows that institutions were explicitly prohibited from using cash management WMPs to finance credit or lending activities that would bypass regulatory restrictions [N4-R3]. It also notes that shadow banking has been a major object of global regulatory attention since the 2008 crisis, with Basel III and other regulations slowing its global growth, yet the 2023 banking crises suggest that regulatory barriers do not fully eliminate systemic vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. The shadow banking paper further highlights that regulatory scrutiny and tightening can reduce apparent growth, but shadow banking may still remain a significant source of financial stability concerns because it often lacks deposit guarantees and central bank liquidity backstop [N4-F3]. In the institutional setting, shadow banking appears to be a shadow finance layer that interacts with traditional banking through interbank and repo-like mechanisms, while regulators attempt to constrain it through WMP restrictions and monitoring frameworks [N4-R4].

Empirically, the evidence supports a pattern in which stronger relationships are associated with greater risk spillovers. The study on interbank lending and systemic risk in China uses the HITS algorithm to analyze network structure and explores the influence of nonbanking institutions [N1-R1]. Another study proposes a DAG-based framework for generalized variance decomposition to investigate heterogeneous return spillovers, showing that network structure and interconnectedness matter for risk transmission [N1-R2]. A third study finds that indirect linkages contribute more to systemic risk than direct linkages, and that different shocks can produce different systemic risk outcomes [N1-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that financial relationships that are more concentrated, more interconnected, or more indirect are more likely to transmit risk. The shadow banking evidence also supports this: shadow banking’s large bond holdings and balance-sheet mismatch make it vulnerable in distress, and its exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing means it can spill over to non-banks and small regional banks [N4-F3]. So the empirical pattern is that stronger, more indirect, and more concentrated relationships—whether in interbank lending, repo, or shadow banking—are associated with larger risk spillovers.

Overall, the institutional context is one of regulated banking coexisting with shadow banking, with interbank and bond-based linkages as the main channels. The regulatory framework tries to limit risky financing and WMP use, but the evidence suggests that even regulated institutions can resemble shadow banking in their business model and vulnerability structure [N4-F3]. The empirical literature indicates that networked relationships—especially those involving indirect exposures, high centrality, and concentration—tend to amplify systemic risk [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

The evidence identifies three main transmission channels: interbank lending, repo, and securitization, each with distinct risk mechanisms. For interbank lending, the ECB paper notes that risk can be transmitted through direct contagion channels due to contractual obligations, but also through indirect mechanisms such as fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes that interbank lending helps banks manage liquidity risk, but also creates vulnerabilities because of the contractual links and the network topology [N3-R3]. The evidence therefore suggests that interbank lending transmits risk by both direct contractual obligations and indirect network effects, with contagion intensity depending on the strength of the shock and the network structure [N3-F2][N3-R3].

For repo, the evidence is indirect but still informative. The ECB paper itself does not directly discuss repo, but it does describe the broader mechanism of collateralized and unsecured interbank markets, where secured and unsecured markets function differently in the presence of credit risk [N3-R4]. The paper also notes that risk transmission can involve liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts, which are especially relevant when institutions face liquidity strains [N3-F2]. While repo is not explicitly modeled here, the collateral and liquidity structure implied by the evidence supports the idea that repo-like transactions can transmit risk through collateral depreciation and liquidity reallocation, especially when institutions have high exposures and face funding stress [N3-R4][N3-F2].

For securitization, the evidence is again indirect but very relevant. The “Securitized Banking and the Run on Repo” paper uses a novel dataset on securitized bonds to trace the path of crisis from subprime-housing related assets into broader markets [N3-R2]. This implies that securitization can transmit risk through asset-backed claims and structured products, with contagion occurring as asset values fall and investors or counterparties become exposed to defaults or liquidity runs [N3-R2]. The broader ECB paper similarly notes that fire sales and depressed asset values can feed into bank balance sheets and risk realization in correlated portfolios, reinforcing the idea that securitized assets can serve as a conduit for risk propagation [N3-F2]. So the evidence supports a view of securitization as a channel where risk moves from underlying collateralized assets into the repo or trading markets, then spreads through interconnected institutions.

The evidence also shows how different loan types and collateral structures change contagion patterns. The ECB paper stresses that secured and unsecured markets function differently under credit risk, with safe collateral, for example, affecting the risk profile of interbank exposures [N3-R4]. The shadow banking study adds that shadow banking often relies on bond holdings and trust financing, and that its balance-sheet mismatch and exposure to commercial real estate and infrastructure financing make it vulnerable in distress [N4-F3]. This means that collateralized lending tends to reduce direct contagion, while unsecured or highly leveraged lending increases vulnerability. The multi-layer financial network study further shows that when banks hold more assets in a single market, they become more vulnerable to that market’s risks [N5-F4]. So the contagion pattern is not uniform: secured or diversified collateral structures can dampen propagation, while concentrated or unsecured exposures can amplify it.

Liquidity and information asymmetry are repeatedly identified as amplifiers of systemic effects. The ECB paper explicitly states that liquidity hoarding, pro-cyclical haircuts, and time-varying risk aversion operate across the banking network [N3-F2]. It also notes that asymmetric information and updating imperfect information or beliefs are key indirect contagion mechanisms [N3-F2]. The shadow banking study similarly points to asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control as vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. These factors combine to make liquidity shocks and information gaps especially dangerous. When institutions face liquidity strains, they may hoard funding, raise haircuts, and propagate risk more rapidly [N3-F2]. When information is incomplete or asymmetric, institutions may misprice risks or fail to update beliefs correctly, which can trigger cascading failures [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a view in which liquidity stress and information asymmetry do not just add noise; they can significantly magnify systemic effects by making contagion more abrupt and harder to contain.

In summary, the risk transmission channels in the evidence are interbank lending (direct and indirect), repo-like collateral and liquidity mechanisms, and securitization-based asset-backed contagion. Different loan types and collateral structures alter contagion patterns: secured and diversified exposures tend to reduce propagation, while unsecured or concentrated exposures amplify it. Liquidity stress and information asymmetry are especially important because they can turn modest shocks into systemic amplification through hoarding, haircuts, and belief updating [N3-F2][N3-R4][N4-F3].

Branch report on systemic risk measurement and modeling frameworks

The evidence identifies several risk measures that are best suited to capturing interconnectedness and failure propagation. CoVaR is a prominent one: the financial network paper states that systemic risk contribution is measured with CoVaR, estimated by applying dynamic conditional correlation multivariate GARCH (DCC-MVGARCH) [N2-R1][N2-F1]. It also notes that CoVaR is defined as the value at risk of the financial system conditional on institutions being under distress [N2-F1]. Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and delta CoVaR are also mentioned in the systematic risk review literature [N2-R2]. In addition, the network paper highlights that financial institutions’ local topology structure affects their systemic risk contribution, and that node strength, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and clustering coefficient are all associated with larger systemic risk contributions [N2-R3][N2-F1]. This suggests that network-based measures such as centrality metrics are useful for capturing interconnectedness, while CoVaR-like measures capture the conditional tail risk of the entire system.

Network-based models differ from traditional VaR/CVaR approaches in two main ways. First, they explicitly model the structure of financial linkages and how those linkages propagate risk across the system. The financial network paper says that financial links are represented as a network, and that empirical or simulation techniques are used to assess failure propagation [N2-F1]. It also notes that the network literature has concentrated on the effects of overall network structure, but that local topology structure and systemic risk contributions have been underexplored [N2-F1]. Second, network models can capture indirect contagion and the role of network topology, whereas traditional VaR and CVaR approaches typically focus on the distributional properties of individual institutions or portfolios [N2-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that indirect contagion can have a much larger upper bound and can dominate contagion effects during severe shocks, which traditional VaR/CVaR approaches may not fully reflect [N3-F2]. Thus, network models are better suited to understanding how interconnectedness and network structure shape systemic risk, while traditional measures are more limited to aggregate risk quantification.

Distinguishing direct contagion from indirect macroeconomic effects is important because the evidence shows that contagion is not always purely internal. The ECB paper explicitly distinguishes direct contagion channels due to contractual obligations from indirect mechanisms such as fire sales, depressed asset values, correlated portfolios, asymmetric information, and updating imperfect information or beliefs [N3-F2]. It also notes that the impact of indirect contagion can be subject to threshold effects and can increase abruptly when thresholds are exceeded, while direct contagion increases gradually with shock intensity [N3-F2]. The same paper states that shocks to sovereign debt and non-bank financial institutions are among the most significant risks to the functioning of the interbank market [N3-F2]. This implies that direct contagion is driven by the network of contractual exposures and funding dependencies, while indirect effects can emerge from broader macroeconomic shocks, asset price declines, and information frictions. The network paper further distinguishes systemic risk contribution from the network structure, showing that local topology matters in addition to macroeconomic conditions [N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered approach: CoVaR and delta CoVaR are useful for tail risk and conditional systemic risk, while network-based measures such as minimum spanning trees and local topology metrics help capture interconnectedness and failure propagation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1]. Traditional VaR/CVaR approaches are less effective at capturing indirect contagion and the role of network structure, which is why network models are better suited to systemic risk assessment in highly interconnected systems [N2-F1][N3-F2]. Direct contagion is tied to contractual obligations and funding links, while indirect contagion and macroeconomic effects arise from asset values, information asymmetry, and broader systemic shocks [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore provides a clear framework for choosing risk measures and distinguishing between direct and indirect sources of systemic risk.

Branch report on multilayer and dynamic contagion mechanisms

The evidence shows that multilayer models represent different financial linkages and exposures by explicitly separating multiple types of connections within the same system. The multi-layer financial network study constructs a model based on three types of links: firm-bank credit, asset-bank portfolio, and interbank lending [N5-R2][N5-F4]. It then simulates systemic risk under three risk sources: firm credit default, asset depreciation, and bank bankruptcy [N5-F4]. This is a clear example of a multilayer representation: each layer captures a distinct financial relationship, so the model can assess how risk spreads through credit, portfolio, and interbank channels simultaneously [N5-F4]. The same paper also notes that financial risk can be spread directly between banks through interbank lending, but that different financial network systems typically have distinct structural characteristics [N5-F4]. This suggests that multilayer models are useful because they avoid the limitations of single-layer analyses and instead capture the full diversity of exposures in a financial system [N5-F4].

Dynamic contagion evolves over time and depends heavily on network structure. The ECB paper emphasizes that its model aims to capture dynamics evolving during crisis rather than tranquil times, and highlights mechanisms such as liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts [N6-R5]. It also states that the impact of indirect contagion can feature threshold effects and can increase abruptly when the threshold is exceeded, while direct contagion increases gradually with shock intensity [N3-F2]. The dynamic multi-layer financial network paper similarly finds that the larger the risk shock, the greater the systemic risk under different risk sources, and that the risk propagation cycle tends to rise and then decline [N5-F4]. This indicates that contagion is not static: it can intensify, then stabilize, and then potentially fade, depending on the shock magnitude and the network structure. The evidence further shows that bank nodes can play both blocking and propagation roles under different risk sources, and that the density of the bank-asset portfolio network, the average degree of firms, and the bank capital adequacy ratio all affect systemic risk [N5-F4]. These findings suggest that dynamic contagion depends not only on the initial shock but also on the evolving network topology and the institutions’ internal characteristics.

Agent-based and BiMM approaches simulate systemic failure propagation by modeling the behavior and interactions of individual agents in a dynamic network. The agent-based multi-layer network simulation paper addresses measuring systemic risk and identifying SIFIs using agent-based methods [N5-R1]. The agent-based model for financial vulnerability paper develops a structure for an agent-based model to provide a system-wide view of agents’ transformations and dynamic interactions [N5-R4]. The multi-layered interbank model paper develops an agent-based multi-layered interbank network model based on a sample of large EU banks [N5-R3]. The multi-agent-based interbank lending network paper generates a dynamic network through a bidirectional matching mechanism (BiMM) [N5-R5]. Together, these sources show that agent-based models simulate systemic failure by representing institutions as agents with rules for behavior, funding, defaulting, and recovery, and by allowing the network to evolve over time [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. BiMM adds a dynamic network generation mechanism, so it can represent both the structure and the time-varying nature of interbank relationships [N5-R5].

The evidence also suggests that multilayer and dynamic models are especially suited to capturing complex contagion patterns. The multi-layer financial network study shows that the system is most susceptible to bank bankruptcy risk, followed by firm credit default risk, and that increasing the density of the bank-asset portfolio network and the capital adequacy ratio can reduce systemic risk [N5-F4]. The dynamic multi-layer financial network paper also finds that the more assets a bank holds in a single market, the more vulnerable it is to the risks associated with that market [N5-F4]. This implies that contagion is not only a matter of network topology but also of asset concentration and exposure diversification. The ECB paper further shows that indirect contagion can dominate during severe shocks, and that liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts amplify propagation [N3-F2]. These findings support the use of multilayer and dynamic models to study how contagion evolves across layers and over time, rather than relying on static snapshots or single-layer assumptions [N5-F4][N5-R5][N3-F2].

In conclusion, multilayer models represent different financial linkages and exposures by separating firm-bank, asset-bank, and interbank layers [N5-R2][N5-F4]. Dynamic contagion evolves over time and depends on network structure, shock magnitude, liquidity conditions, and institutional characteristics [N3-F2][N5-F4]. Agent-based and BiMM approaches simulate systemic failure propagation by representing agents, dynamic interactions, and evolving network structures [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a modeling strategy in which multilayer and dynamic approaches are the most appropriate tools for understanding how risk propagates through interconnected financial systems.

The evidence points to a system dominated by **shadow banking and interbank markets**, with **commercial banks, trust financing, bond holdings, WMPs, and interbank lending** as the most common linkages [N4-F3][N1-R1]. The interbank lending literature further shows that **interbank networks are the primary empirical focus**, and that the structure of these networks is often analyzed using **direct and indirect contagion mechanisms** [N1-R1][N3-F2]. The evidence also implies that **securitization and asset-backed lending** are important transmission channels, because they can bundle risks into structured products and then spread them through interconnected institutions [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Regulation plays a central role in shaping both the types of relationships and the risk profile of the system. It also notes that shadow banking has been a major object of global regulatory attention since the 2008 crisis, with **Basel III and other regulations slowing its global growth**, yet the 2023 banking crises suggest that regulatory barriers do not fully eliminate systemic vulnerabilities [N4-F3]. The shadow banking study highlights that **asset-liability mismatch, risk-oriented investment strategy, and lack of internal control** are vulnerabilities, implying that institutions can become risky if they are not properly regulated or if they rely on complex financing structures [N4-F3]. The empirical evidence strongly supports the view that **stronger relationships are associated with greater risk spillovers**. The shadow banking evidence also supports this pattern. Thus, network models are better suited to understanding how interconnectedness and network structure shape systemic risk [N2-F1][N3-F2].

The ECB paper emphasizes that its model aims to capture **dynamics evolving during crisis rather than tranquil times**, and highlights mechanisms such as **liquidity hoarding and pro-cyclical haircuts** [N6-R5].
